6. The trial court found title and possession in favour of the plaintiff and decreed the suit with costs against defendant No. 1. On appeal, the learned Subordinate Judge set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and allowed the appeal. The plaintiff preferred the Second Appeal in the High Court at Dacca and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division allowed the appeal and restored the trial court's judgment and decree. The defendant No. 1 moved this Court and obtained leave to consider whether the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act, particularly those contained in section 26C which bars all kinds of transfer of agricultural land except in certain cases excluded therein without a registered instrument which does not contain an oral gift by a Muhammedan, would apply in the present case so as to nullify the validity of the oral gift which is the basis of the plaintiff's title. Further, if the oral gift in  favour of the plaintiff on which he relies is hit by section 26C of the Bengal Tenancy Act whether operation of section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act would be excluded. 

 7. Mr. K.A. Bakr, Counsel for the defendant appellant, submitted that since the suit land is agricultural land the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act would apply in case of transfer of the land, section 26C which was inserted by way of amendment in 1928 being prior to the transfer of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff will govern the transfer. No exception to its applicability Can be taken by mentioning that the transfer concerned being by an oral gift is not covered by the word 'transfer'. The expressions used in section 26C include every transfer excepting a bequest or a sale in execution of a decree or of a certificate signed under the Bengal Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913. An oral gift comes within the ambit and scope of "every transfer" mentioned in the section. After the enactment of the State Acquisition and. Tenancy Act, 1950 provisions relating to the transfer of land of a raiyat which are relevant for our purpose are contained in sections 88 and 89 of the Act. Section 88 provides- 

 On a comparison between the provisions of section 26C of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, it would appear that the words used in both sections are identical. Quite obviously, the interpretation of the former will govern the latter as well unless some distinction can be pointed out. 

 10. Reference was made to two other decisions in support of the contention that an oral gift by a Muslim is subject to the provisions of section 26C of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 17 of the Registration Act, both of which require a registered instrument to make the gift of immovable property valid. The first is the case of Antaz Mia vs. Mohammad Mostafa, (1965) 17 DLR 112 which held that from a reading of section 26C it was clear that its provisions were made applicable to the transfer under the Muhammadan Law. Further, though the Bengal Tenancy Act was a Provincial law it received the assent of the Governor General of India, and would, therefore, override the personal laws of Muhammadans. No comparison was made between the provisions of section 26C and section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act. In the second case, namely, Ismail Sayed vs. Commissioner of Karachi, 1968 SCMR 509 the Pakistan Supreme Court, in making a casual observation, said that the suit property being of the value of more than Rs. 100/- no right, title or interest in it could, under section 17 of the Registration Act, be conveyed except by a deed in writing and duly registered. The particular transfer being an oral gift was, therefore, not given effect to in protecting the donee of the gift against ejectment under the relevant law. The observation, made in this decision that oral transfer by gift by a Muslim above hundred rupees required registration is not a correct interpretation of section 17 of the Registration Act. 

 12. The conflict that has, arisen in the present case is not so much between the provisions of tenancy laws regarding transfer. of immovable property and the personal law of Muslim on the same in particular regarding gift of immovable property, but so much of it as has been recognised in the Transfer of Property Act. Section 129 of this Act which has recognised the personal laws of Muslim relating to gifts as follows:- 

 13. Further, the learned Counsel for the appellant laid stress on the distinction between agricultural land and non-agricultural land and the different requirements of the two laws, regarding transfer of such land by gift. It may, however, be mentioned that there is no indication in section 129 restricting its application only to a particular class of lands, that is, non-agricultural land as section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1943 has provided. Section 117 of the Transfer of Property Act excludes from its operation only agricultural leases but not other dispositions. 

 14. So far as the wording of either section 26C of the Bengal Tenancy Act or section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is concerned, we do not find any reference to section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act which read with other sections of this Act contained contrary provisions relating to the requirement of registration of an instrument or gift by a Muslim. If the legislature intended to exclude the operation of section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act by the later enactment, it ought have expressly said so, or could have used some such expressions as notwithstanding anything contained in any ether law for the time being in force". Such phraseology or expressions are used by the legislature to give an enactment or some of its provisions an overriding quality and operation. One does not even have to look up other laws to find the use of such expressions. In section 90 as also in other sections of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act such expressions have been resorted to so as to impart superiority to its provisions over other laws. There is no such clause in section 89 of the Act or section 26C of B.T. Act which is under our consideration so as to exclude the operation of section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act in case of transfer of agricultural land. In addition, after the enactment of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act very little distinctions maintained between the incidents of agricultural land and non-agricultural land. For solid practical reasons also, no such distinction would seem to be attractive. If law as provided in section 129 has exempted the owner of urban property, which are generally more valuable than agricultural land, from transferring the same by a registered instrument, why should greater hardship be imposed on the holder of agricultural and by the requirement of a registered instrument for transferring his, interest therein by way of gift. Judged from different viewpoints, the effectiveness of an oral gift of immovable property when properly made has not been curtailed by the language of section 26C of the Bengal Tenancy Act or section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act insofar as it has been preserved by section 129 of the Transfer of Property Act. An oral gift of immovable property, whether it is agricultural land, or non-agricultural land, made according to the Muslim Law would, therefore be valid.
